claims.text: The starting material consists of crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
Introducing a sacrificial oxide layer such as CeO2 can overcome structural or chemical instability of these nanoparticles during catalytic operation.
The proposed intervention is the introduction of a sacrificial oxide layer, exemplified by CeO2.
The hypothesis is intended to apply throughout 773–1173 K.
The sacrificial oxide layer can undergo oxidation and reduction reactions.
Oxidation and reduction of the oxide layer stabilize the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Oxidation and reduction of the oxide layer prevent structural or chemical instability.
Sub-nanometer CoNiCuZnPd high-entropy-alloy clusters on CeO2 exhibit structural reversibility under repeated oxidative and reductive exposure.
The oxide-treated nanoparticles will have greater stability than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the sacrificial oxide layer.
The oxide-treated nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the sacrificial oxide layer.
Composition and nanoparticle size are boundary conditions for the proposed effect.
In situ XAFS during thermal exposure can be used to assess structural changes in the treated and untreated nanoparticles.
A lack of improvement in both stability and catalytic performance relative to an untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
